evidence.title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
evidence.outcome: clinician acceptance
evidence.effect: Clinicians in the AI-assisted group demonstrated high acceptance with a 92.6% adoption rate.
evidence.quote: In the randomised open-label comparison study, clinicians in the AI-assisted group had a high acceptance of the AI model (92·6% adoption rate), and a higher AUC when compared with the control group (0·858 [95% CI 0·850-0·866] vs 0·789 [0·780-0·799]; p<0·0001).

evidence.title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: identification of interface preference
evidence.effect: revealed a 60% preference for voice interfaces among older or low-literacy users
evidence.quote: In the implementation and evolution phase, a pilot study (20 patients, Beijing) revealed a 60% (12/20) preference for voice interfaces among older/low-literacy users, driving integration of real-time speech-to-text conversion (Fig. 1d ).

evidence.title: Deployment of a human-centred clinical decision support system for pulmonary embolism: evaluation of impact on quality of diagnostic decisions
evidence.outcome: Adherence to evidence-based PE diagnostic pathways before vs after human-centred CDSS deployment
evidence.effect: Overall adherence 0.63 vs 0.60 (p=0.18); D-dimer use 42.9% vs 55.7% (p=0.014) and CTPA use 61.9% vs 75.4% (p=0.005) lower in intervention phase; adherence higher when Wells used.
evidence.quote: Overall adherence to diagnostic pathways was 0.63 in the CDSS intervention phase versus 0.60 in the preintervention phase (p=0.18), with fewer workups in the CDSS intervention phase having very low adherence scores.

evidence.outcome: Clinician acceptance of proposed diagnoses after feedback-informed algorithm adaptations
evidence.effect: Acceptance improved for some diagnoses after adaptations informed by clinician feedback and expert input; numerical before–after effects were not reported.
evidence.quote: A before–after analysis showed improved acceptance for some diagnoses following adaptations.

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-one studies report on pilot usability testing and feedback-driven revision, and most show that feedback changed tool design or raised acceptance and usability scores. None compares tools refined through structured end-user feedback against tools deployed without it on patient outcomes, and the one comparative study found no change in pathway adherence.

perspectives.view: The two randomized trials measure clinician acceptance or interface preference inside an AI trial rather than comparing feedback-informed with uninformed deployment. The only comparative test of a human-centred tool found adherence of 0.63 versus 0.60 (p=0.18). The remaining studies are uncontrolled pre-post, qualitative, or simulated designs with user-reported outcomes, so certainty is very low.

Hazard studies show that burdensome multistage workflows led to ignored alerts and unplaced orders, and that monthly clinician use of one tool fell from 88.7% to 66.2%. In one pilot, end-user interviews led designers to exclude certain patients and allow clinicians to refuse recommendations. This suggests feedback may catch fit problems early, though no study links such changes to fewer harms.

Iterative feedback raised usability from 47.9 to 69.3 on the System Usability Scale in one study, and 93% of clinicians adopted a search tool after a user-centered rollout. Another team used human-centered design and still saw 3% utilization in the first three months. These results suggest that feedback processes improve ratings but do not reliably produce use.

One trial that enrolled older, rural, low-literacy, and limited English proficiency participants found a 60% preference for voice interfaces among older or low-literacy users. In a Danish study of 20 patients, preference for human translation fell from 90% to 50% after patient face validation. These findings suggest that testing with representative users may surface needs that clinician-only testing would miss.

Clinicians used 17.5% of AI-drafted patient messages in one system, and a later prompt revision informed by feedback raised patient preference for drafts from under 15% to 62%. A Dutch rollout lost 9% of practices in eight weeks and reported that assistants were under-involved in design. These studies suggest that omitting some user groups may carry retention costs.

Few studies asked patients directly. In South Africa, 100 community members gave a simulated HIV tool a mean usability score of 81.6, and 94.9% said they would use it again. Patient preference for message drafts rose after revision. These results suggest that patients can give usable feedback, but none of the studies measured trust or patients' access to a human.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to show that users can operate the device and interpret its output in the actual context of clinical decision-making. CHAI guidance asks whether user acceptance testing is both qualitative and quantitative. No supplied study tests whether meeting these expectations changes outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomizes or otherwise compares deployments that did and did not use structured end-user feedback before full rollout while measuring sustained use, errors, or patient outcomes, and few studies report how representative the tested users were.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests included limited English proficiency or non-English users, and one of these also included low-literacy, rural, and older adults, but all three took place in China or Denmark, and two used offline or simulated settings. No test enrolled Medicaid or U.S. safety-net populations, so the evidence does not show whether pilot feedback processes capture the needs of those users.
